speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head N of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: During the Cold War, China and the United States (US) were on opposite sides, with relations only thawing under President Nixon and Secretary Henry Kissinger who visited China and met with Chairman Mao in the early 1970s.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the 1980s and 1990s, relations continued to thaw as China integrated itself into the world economy, culminating in its membership of the World Trade Organization in 2001.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Both countries prospered together for much of the time since, with trade and capital flowing across.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: China has since grown to become the second largest economy in the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Along with its economic growth, it has developed as a military power and a major player on the international stage – with its Belt and Road Initiative providing investment and engagement far and wide.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As discussed in this House in previous Committee of Supply (COS) debates, Singapore watches the trajectory of US-China relations closely.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The issue of Taiwan also continues to be a potential tinderbox in relations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our global economy is inter-dependent and any bifurcation between the two largest economic powers will be painful.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This can only lead to a more fractured, more divided, less prosperous and less peaceful world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In matters, such as climate change, US and China are the world's largest carbon producers and as these matters need a collective solution, it will be important for the US and China to demonstrate leadership in these issues.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore and Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) are both in a difficult position in this matter, as we have close economic and political ties to both countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Considering the current state of geopolitics, how can Singapore preserve our relevance to both the US and China without choosing sides?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Chairperson, Sir, the world remains deeply divided as we start 2024.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Geopolitically speaking, the world has yet to emerge from long COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Both the Russian Ukraine war and the Israeli-Hamas conflict shows no signs of abating and could escalate beyond.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: US-China rivalry remains heightened, with both major powers mired in complex internal complications.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Trade tensions between the major trading blocs continue to rise over semiconductors and electric vehicles; and global warming continues unabated, because the world lacks a strong collective will to fight it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, the stable geopolitical backdrop and international trading system – that served Singapore well for decades – continue to dissipate.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Given these increasing geopolitical divisions, how can Singapore continue to maintain our relevance and our ability to make independent foreign policy decisions?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And because foreign policy starts at home, can the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) share on what more can be done to unite our people behind our foreign policy decisions so that we can advance our collective interests as one people?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, the current international state of affairs has been marked by multiple sources of disruption and turbulence.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are ongoing conflicts in various regions of the world, including Europe and the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In an interconnected world, these conflicts have had a significant economic and emotional impact on our people.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Geopolitical competition between large powers have created centrifugal forces that are affecting many countries in a major way.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have shifted away from a unipolar world order – as it was in the 1990s and 2000s.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are entering a period of reduced strategic trust and increased suspicion between the large powers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This has increased the need for Singapore to diversify our economic partnerships with the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has also become a major source of technological disruption.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is clear that even in the arena of international affairs, it cannot be business as usual.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore must be nimble and identify the opportunities and risks that AI and other frontier technologies will bring.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The international rules for AI are also nascent.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a small but highly globalised city-state, how can we ensure that Singapore's foreign policy remains independent and is future-proofed and fit for purpose to overcome these challenges in this new age?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, the Gaza war shows no signs of abating and this conflict is now spilling to other parts of the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In October 2023, the Houthis, ostensibly in condemnation of Israel's military operation in the Gaza, launched unlawful attacks on vessels in the Red Sea region, a major sea line of communication (SLOC).

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This has disrupted the flow of trade and threatened the safety and freedom of navigation through the area.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As a maritime and trading nation, it is in our interest to work with the international community to uphold international law and ensure that SLOC in the Red Sea remain open.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Given our reliance on maritime trade routes, what more does Singapore plan to do in relation to this issue?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Chairman, many Singaporeans are distressed by the humanitarian situation in Gaza.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: All sides should do their utmost to prioritise the safety of civilians and stop the attacks and destruction of civilian infrastructure.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To protect their sovereignty and their peoples' livelihoods, countries have the right to self-defence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: That said, all countries must respond proportionately and respect international law.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This is essential for the international community to provide humanitarian aid that the civilians of Gaza urgently need.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Given the continued crisis, what else can Singapore do to address the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has had a long history of being a multicultural and globalised society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A large part of our success as a nation can be attributed to how we have celebrated our diversity and lived in harmony.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our citizens are comfortable on digital platforms, travel widely and consume a wide array of media from many different countries.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That said, we should remain clear-eyed about the potential downsides and work proactively to mitigate them.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Foreign actors may attempt to interfere in our way of life via influence operations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If left unchecked, this may disrupt our balanced societal fabric.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As such, it is vital for Singapore to guard against external players that seek to influence our society and advance certain perspectives that may cause division.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MFA plays an important role and, here, I place on record my thanks to MFA officers who have worked hard on the ground and overseas to fly the Singapore flag high.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can Singapore preserve our racial and religious harmony and remain vigilant against foreign interference?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, the worsening humanitarian situation in Gaza has evoked strong reactions amongst many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am reassured that many Singaporeans have made significant contributions through donations in cash and other forms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How else has Singapore contributed to resolving the humanitarian situation in the Israel-Hamas conflict?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, as a small country, the existence of a rules-based international order meant a lot to us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is where we derive stability and normality and, hence, peace and prosperity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: From my understanding of what rules-based international order is, a major part seems to centre on the United Nations (UN) and its Charter.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: A hundred and ninety three countries have signed to be part of the UN Charter and, hence, are obliged to follow the principles and provisions that extend from that Charter.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides the UN Charter, there are other international conventions, treaties, international agreements and rulings from the ICJ which purported to be rules that nations should abide by.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Notwithstanding all these rules and international agreements that we have, we know that there is no shortage of violations or unobserved rules by countries big or small.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There appears to be no supranational enforcement body that can reign in any violations of all these rules.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Under this setting, how can tiny Singapore play our part to bolster the rules-based international order?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, geopolitical tensions around the world are high, including the Russia-Ukraine war and the Israel-Palestine crisis in Gaza, among others.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They threaten the foundation of a rules-based international order crucial to Singapore's existence.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have made efforts to speak up and participate at multilateral forums, but in a world where size and might threaten to dominate, we cannot just seek to maintain peace, but must make active efforts towards building it.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Small states may naturally face challenges at platforms, such as the UN, because of our relative size.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have found coalition through informal groups with like-minded members, such as the Forum of Small States.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such groupings allow us to better register our interests and concerns in one voice.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In ASEAN, how are we supporting efforts to strengthen integration between member states to ensure that the platform remains relevant and fit for purpose, translating into effective actions that benefit us both as Singapore and as a collective bloc?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, my cut concerns Singapore's work with other small states.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Small states, by their very nature, share specific concerns and common interests, such as environmental and economic vulnerabilities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has historically supported platforms that allow small states to discuss and foster common positions on issues of mutual concern.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Accordingly, this gives all parties involved a much bigger voice in the United Nations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have strong ties at the political, economic and people-to-people levels.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our Government have engaged Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim consistently over many years and have maintained regular exchanges between political officeholders and senior officials.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As such, we enjoy good relations with Malaysia, with mutual interest and commitment to deepen engagement and expand cooperation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are also initiatives, such as the ASEAN Power Grid, which will strengthen regional interconnectivity and enhance energy security for both countries.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would MFA share how we can ensure continuity and growth in our bilateral cooperation with Malaysia?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the current state of global affairs is relatively turbulent, characterised by competition between major powers and multiple crises happening around the world.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It, therefore, remains important for Singapore, as a small country, to contribute towards building regional stability, including through working with our closest neighbours.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: What areas can we specifically contribute to in the near term?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has also worked with Malaysia on many projects, some of which have been focused on Johor.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: JS-SEZ aims to strengthen connectivity through improving the cross-border flows of goods and people between both sides of the Causeway.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, I understand that Singapore has also been working with Malaysia on easing congestion at the Causeway.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, Singapore has always sought to maintain good relationships with our neighbouring countries.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We and our fellow ASEAN Member States have common interests in preserving regional peace and stability.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: ASEAN countries have great potential for economic growth, particularly in emerging areas, such as renewable energy, carbon credits and the digital economy, where there is room for cooperation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They have growing young and energetic populations and significant natural resources that provide ample opportunities for collaboration, such as the agri-food sector.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Two of our closest neighbours, Malaysia and Indonesia, have seen or will be seeing political transitions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Malaysia, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's Unity Government has been in power for over a year now.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While we have already been working closely with both Malaysia and Indonesia, there remains to be many new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Both nations have a younger demographic than Singapore and larger domestic markets.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have deep and longstanding defence relations with Thailand and have strengthened cooperation in the digital economy realm through initiatives, such as the PayNow-PromptPay Linkage.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our strategic partnership with Vietnam may be upgraded to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in the future.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we embark on our decarbonisation agenda, the Lao PDR-Thailand-Malaysia-Singapore Power Integration Project (LTMS-PIP) has paved the way for us to begin importing renewable energy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Minister give us an overview of the state of our relationships with our neighbours?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What more can Singapore do to deepen her engagements with Southeast Asian countries beyond our immediate neighbours?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What new areas of cooperation should we focus on to ensure that Singapore remains well-positioned to work fruitfully with them?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, during these turbulent times, it is important for Singapore to keep our existing partnerships strong while seeking to expand our network.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Singapore has strong people-to-people and economic ties with Indonesia across many sectors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: How is the Government supporting and nurturing these relationships?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: In view of the upcoming change in leadership, how will we continue to pursue a positive agenda with Indonesia?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Singapore is an important gateway for foreign investments into Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: We are also exploring emerging areas of cooperation in areas, such as renewable energy, healthcare and carbon capture and storage.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Amidst shifting global supply chains, we should do more with Indonesia on food security cooperation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: With so much potential at hand, how can we ensure that our relationship with Indonesia remains robust and that both sides continue to work together in the spirit of cooperation?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, our relationship with Indonesia, our immediate neighbour and the largest economy in ASEAN, has been an important one.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: We have had strong ties with successive Presidents and built relationships at all levels, including between our governments, militaries, businesses and at the people-to-people level.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Indonesia was, together with us, among the founding members of ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: After almost 10 years, Indonesia will now be undergoing a leadership transition.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: President Jokowi has been a popular President, and during his time, we have achieved some significant milestones in the relationship, including signing agreements to address the flight information region (FIR), defence cooperation and an extradition treaty.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Indonesia held its presidential election on 14 February this year, and Defence Minister Prabowo Subianto appears to have won a convincing majority.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I understand that General Prabowo is well-known to many of our leaders and I believe it will be important for us to build deeper ties with the new administration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: How will Singapore continue to maintain good ties with the new administration and what opportunities does MFA see to deepen ties further with Indonesia?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Indochina is the region of ASEAN that sits between India and China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Our relationship with Thailand is a long-standing one – as a fellow founding ASEAN member.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: We have deep and longstanding defence relations with Thailand and have strengthened cooperation in the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The other countries in Indochina – Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos – are newer members of ASEAN, with whom we also have also steadily built ties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: We have a strategic partnership with Vietnam and are exploring upgrading relations to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: There are growing opportunities for us to collaborate in emerging areas, such as renewable energy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The Lao PDR-Thailand-Malaysia-Singapore Power Integration Project (LTMS-PIP) is an example.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This allows us to import renewable energy and could be a pathfinder for an eventual ASEAN Power Grid.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I will be interested to know if MFA has any update on the status of relations with Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos and its plan for the upcoming year?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Chairman, will MFA provide an update on our diplomatic and economic relations with the countries in Indochina region – Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and Thailand?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: What are the current and upcoming projects in trade, investment and regional cooperation, such as digital finance initiatives with Thailand and the decarbonisation projects with Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore and Laos are fellow small states who have worked well together.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: We should further deepen cooperation with Timor-Leste in capacity-building once we establish our resident Mission in Dili.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: What more can we do to help Laos and Timor-Leste and build caring communities in ASEAN and beyond?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: What can the people and private sectors do to support these efforts?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, the conditions in Myanmar following the military coup in 2021 are not improving.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The civil war appears to be turning more intense with the military suffering territorial losses, the attacking of civilians and more lately, the decision to conscript the male population.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This despite ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus and efforts to reach to the military leadership of the State Administration Council as well as apparent informal contact with the National Unity Government.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How with the change in ASEAN Chair affect the progress made so far?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Events in Myanmar may seem far away from Singapore to some.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, given that Myanmar is a regional neighbour, our fates are linked.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Civil war in Myanmar has also led to rising human trafficking, expanded drug production, increased drug trafficking and what looks like an exponential growth in scams.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some of these scams allegedly originate from Myanmar.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Singaporeans have also been ensnared by crime syndicates and forced to work for scam operations in Myanmar.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If we are concerned about tackling drugs, human trafficking and scams in Singapore, we should also be concerned to see how more efforts should be made to address some of the roots of this problem.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: That also means – among other things – supporting Myanmar's return to stability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are both humanitarian and practical reasons for doing so, as I laid out above.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is also easy enough to ignore what is happening in Myanmar, as conflicts in Gaza and Ukraine continue to rage.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But what goes on in Myanmar has arguably more direct consequences for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With the worsening situation in Myanmar, how does MFA intend to address the multiple challenges that Myanmar poses to Singapore and the region in the coming year – whether by ourselves or in conjunction with our ASEAN partners?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will MFA also be officially engaging the National Unity Government and other groups opposed to the State Administration Council?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These actors are, in the end, key stakeholders too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How will MFA work with our ASEAN partners to concretely address any limitations of the Five-Point Consensus process?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, it has been three years since the coup in Myanmar and conditions for the people of Myanmar remain dire.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singapore has strongly supported ASEAN's efforts to provide urgent humanitarian assistance for the people of Myanmar, including through the ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance on Disaster Management (AHA Centre).

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: We have made a variety of contributions through the AHA Centre and also provided assistance when Cyclone Mocha hit Myanmar in May 2023.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This included the RSAF's delivery of the AHA Centre's relief supplies to Myanmar, using our C-130 aircraft.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singapore has stated that it will continue to work with fellow ASEAN member states to support the AHA Centre.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: However, other than humanitarian assistance, does MFA believe there is anything else Singapore and ASEAN can and should do to help resolve the crisis in Myanmar?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Can anything else be done to address the humanitarian issues in Myanmar?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Chairman, there has been greater emphasis and high visibility of ASEAN in our regional affairs in recent years and, at the same time, many of the ASEAN member states have also been playing prominent roles in their own way.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: In past Committee of Supply debates, the issue of ASEAN centrality comes up quite often.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: ASEAN is the often seen as the representational regional grouping that speak in one voice on regional issues and engage with external powers as a unified group.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: We all know that ASEAN can only stay relevant and influential if there are unity of purpose and member states seeing strength in its collective value.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It provided a means for regional states to de-emphasise differences and work together – both during the Cold War and after.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Much of the foreign direct investment coming into Singapore is then reinvested in other ASEAN member states to the benefit of our economy and businesses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For a long time, ASEAN centrality was based around its ability to convene events that bring together different, even rival actors around the world.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was a way for Singapore and fellow members to amplify our voices internationally.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are increasing questions about improving and maintaining internal cohesion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, the intensifying US-PRC rivalry has also put pressure on the governments, societies and interests of different ASEAN members to move in divergent directions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Conditions may well get worse, given the continued trouble for the Chinese economy and US domestic politics leading up to and following the elections in November this year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These circumstances mean that more than ever, Singapore and fellow ASEAN members need an ASEAN that is suited for the times.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How do we make the concept of ASEAN centrality more concrete, such that it has a continued ability to set regional agendas and perhaps even bargain collectively?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What are plans to collaborate with other extra-regional partners to augment the work of ASEAN in defence of Singapore's interests?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If we are committed to the ASEAN project, then we must make it work.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, Singapore is a strong supporter and an active and founding member of ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Amidst a troubled global outlook, it is even more important for Singapore to take the lead and work with ASEAN member states to pursue a positive agenda and deliver substantive cooperation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, what can Singapore do to support Laos' Chairmanship through the year?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, the Middle East continues to be a key region of importance for Singapore and the world.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Over the years, we have cultivated strong ties with many Gulf countries and have had frequent high-level exchanges.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In October 2023, our Prime Minister visited Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: If I may ask the Minister: how does Singapore plan to build on these high-level engagements to strengthen further our relations and cooperation with the Gulf countries?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, what are some emerging areas of collaboration with the Gulf countries that have embraced economic transformation and diversification?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Chairman, Singapore is a strategic partner of South Africa.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Many major South African companies have their Asian headquarters here.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Last year, our Prime Minister made his first official visit to South Africa while South African Deputy President made an official visit to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: How is our relationship with South Africa and how do we see our engagement with the broader African region?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Chairman, the ongoing competition and tensions between the United States and China have intensified in recent years, particularly in economic, technological and geopolitical spheres.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore, as a small, open economy strategically located in Southeast Asia, is deeply affected by the dynamics between the US and China.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the US-China rivalry continues to evolve, Singapore will need to navigate carefully to mitigate risks while seizing opportunities that emerge from this contestation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our ability to maintain neutrality, adapt to changing economic and geopolitical landscapes and leverage our strengths will be crucial in safeguarding its interests amidst the US-China competition.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yet, Singapore will continue to face pressures from both sides to take side.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How will Singapore manage such pressures and ensure that Singapore's national interest continues to be safeguarded?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In addition, as a sovereign country, Singapore must decide our own path and destiny.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We take pride in Singapore being multiracial and multicultural.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Throughout history, we have seen how certain divisive narratives and perspectives can create major rifts in societies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore must guard against these divisive narratives, lest they create schisms between Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some of these messages can come from foreign sources and perhaps, with an intent to influence which side our country should take.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this digital age, messages can spread more quickly and it is getting difficult to discern the accuracy and intent of information.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Deepfakes can also become more prevalent, making the challenge worse and our democracy can also be greatly undermined.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, how will our Government manage and reduce such risk of foreign influence in our domestic politics?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This was an important milestone that affirmed the longstanding and mutually beneficial partnership that we share.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It reflects our mutual commitment to deepen and refresh our wide-ranging cooperation – including in new and emerging areas.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Our cooperation is anchored by institutional mechanisms, such as the three government-to-government projects: Suzhou Industrial Park, Tianjin Eco-City and Chongqing Connectivity Initiative.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Both sides kept a high tempo of bilateral exchanges throughout 2023.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore welcomed several senior PRC leaders in 2023, including Vice-President Han Zheng last November and Foreign Minister Wang Yi last August.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In turn, many Singapore delegations have visited China, including Prime Minister in March, Deputy Prime Minister Wong in May and December, and several other Ministers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, what is our outlook for China in 2024 and in the long term?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Mr Chairman, that the rivalry between Washington and Beijing is becoming more and more serious is undeniable, as are other points of friction in East Asia and beyond.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: One of the Deputy Prime Ministers also raised the issue on several occasions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Competition among major powers is a common feature of their relations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Well managed, they can spur innovation and grow within stable and predictable parameters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: If not, contestation can prompt friction, tension, instability, unpredictability and an extreme conflict.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: A key element of US-China ties today is marked by the US and its allies on one side, China and its partners on the other.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Contentiousness is growing in the arc from the Korean Peninsula and the Sea of Japan, through the East Asia Sea, the Taiwan Strait and the South China Sea.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Ships and aircraft are challenging established norms and interpretations of international law, even as these areas are seeing greater militarisation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: In the process, ships and aircraft from different sides are increasingly emboldened, or perhaps ordered to adopt riskier manoeuvres.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Left unattended, current developments could spell greater instability in the region, perhaps even crisis and confrontation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Of course, no one expects Singapore to do anything about the increasingly tense regional atmosphere on our own.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: That said, it is in Singapore's interest to work with various partners to encourage better management of tensions before they get worse and more difficult to contain.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Could the Minister explain to this House and the public the efforts that MFA is undertaking towards this end?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: What is the MFA doing to work with fellow ASEAN members and other partners to reduce the growing risk?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: As a smaller actor, Singapore may have to be a price taker to conditions created by others, but we have the benefits of agility and relative unity given our size.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: How does MFA propose that we use these advantages to secure Singapore and protect our interests in a more uncertain and tumultuous time?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This may be a test of our wisdom and capability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: In the event differences among the different sides should escalate, how does MFA propose that Singapore mitigate the elevated risk that may result?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Pressure from various parties and major powers is likely to mount on Singapore under these circumstances.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: They will come externally and may even emerge internally.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The public needs to understand this risk, be prepared for a response and be ready to support it, including accepting the cost mitigation efforts which may entail and what might these be.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The US remain the undisputed leader in the global economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: She continues to attract the world's top technology, finance, biotechnology and creative talent.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The US continues to defy its critics and re-invent itself economically constantly, as demonstrated by its commanding lead in the recent artificial intelligence (AI) revolution.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The US dollar remains the sole world reserve currency due to the depth, transparency and productivity of the America's capital markets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: And over the last decade, by developing her shale oil and natural gas industries, the US has become a net energy exporter, which lessens its dependence on energy from the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: As such, more economists are revising their views of the US' place in the world and expect the US to remain the largest world economy for years, despite her much smaller population compared to India and China.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: At the same time, the past and current US governments is committed to redrawing its supply chain, and more importantly, re-thinking its relations with its world.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore's relationships with two global powerhouses, China and India, are pivotal to ensuring continued economic growth and the provision of good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: China stands as one of Singapore's largest trading partners and our robust economic relations continue to thrive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, China is undergoing major economic changes and growth has declined.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are also greater demographic changes due to an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Geopolitical tensions are also disrupting trade and supply chains.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An area in which China has excelled is sustainable development.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: China today is the largest producer of solar panels and electric vehicles.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can Singapore businesses enhance cooperation with China in the area of environmental sustainability?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Similarly, Singapore's relationship with India is anchored in historical, cultural, and economic connections.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: India represents a vibrant democracy, a fast-growing economy and a rich cultural heritage.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, we recognise that challenges exist in our relationships with both China and India.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Geopolitical tensions and evolving strategic interests that at times conflict will require us to navigate carefully and adapt dynamically to changing circumstances.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In recent years, China and India have also exhibited newfound confidence and assertiveness in their foreign policies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How do we ensure that Singapore remains steadfast and consistent in our relations with China and India?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Concurrently, how do we continue to deepen people-to-people exchanges and how do we build cultural knowledge of our people, especially our young, so that Singaporeans can build long-lasting relationships anchored by mutual trust and respect?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Since COVID-19, many countries have begun to reconfigure their economic strategies to shield themselves from external shocks.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Practices such as "near-shoring" have disrupted the established global supply chains.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Singapore must remain adaptable and find new ways to enhance our economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: We should strengthen cooperation with new partners around to world to diversify our supplies of critical commodities and remain relevant to the global economy.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: How has Singapore widened our network to enhance economic resilience and promote greater economic integration?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: The global economic environment has become more uncertain in recent years.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Even as we deepen cooperation with our traditional partners, Singapore should do more to strengthen its links with other global players.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: There are new economic opportunities in emerging markets that Singapore can tap on, both regionally and further afield.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: We have complementary strengths and shared interests in cooperating with these diverse partners on supply chain resilience, the green and digital economies, as well as renewable energy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: We must work to diversify Singapore's options and expand our network of friends around the world.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: This will mitigate the external shocks and challenges brought about by an increasingly fragmented world.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: How is Singapore building relations and trade links with new and emerging markets?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Countries have reacted by trying to bring critical supply chains closer to home through "near-shoring".

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Rising geopolitical tensions have also caused countries to look at economic issues through a strategic lens.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Emerging technologies have impacted many aspects of our lives and many industries have successfully incorporated it in their workstreams.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For MFA, one key workstream is the provision of consular services to Singaporeans in need.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Has MFA used technology to improve the provision of consular services in recent years?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Singapore Cooperation Programme is Singapore's flagship platform for technical cooperation with developing countries.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is Singapore's way of paying forward the assistance we received from other countries and international organisations in our early years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Can MFA provide an update on how it is supporting the capacity building of other countries through the Singapore Cooperation Programme?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For overseas Singaporeans who get into distress, having access to MFA's consular services becomes critical.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am glad to note that the hon Minister for Foreign Affairs has gone on record to stress that assisting overseas Singaporeans is a priority for his Ministry.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What steps has MFA taken in this regard?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How was technology leveraged to provide a better quality of consular services to Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How does MFA assess Singaporeans' satisfaction level of consular services rendered to them?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With the rise in media coverage of fluid and potentially divisive global issues, Singaporeans are engaging in discussions on foreign policy more actively than ever before.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This growing trend not only reflects a heightened interest in global affairs but also underscores the importance of such conversations for a nation that is significantly influenced by international events.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, while this increased interest is positive, there is still room for improvement in how the Government communicates the underlying considerations of foreign policy to the public.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Diplomacy and foreign policy are complex and multi-faceted with various conflicting perspectives.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Every decision or statement made can have far-reaching consequences for Singapore's open economy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Therefore, it is crucial for MFA to regularly involve Singaporeans in discussions to foster a clearer understanding of the country's fundamental interests in foreign policy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A united and well-informed citizenry is essential for the success of our foreign policy endeavours.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In light of this, I would like to inquire about MFA's plans to engage Singaporeans on foreign policy matters to enhance awareness of Singapore's core interests.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: What approaches are being taken to ensure the prompt and accurate sharing of information, facilitating constructive dialogue, and enhancing resilience among our citizens and businesses?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How do these actions reinforce Singapore's international position, protect our national interests and maintain economic stability?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Chairman, thank you for all the contributions, questions, suggestions from Members of Parliament (MPs).

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Again, this year I was struck by the fact that the speeches of the Opposition and the Nominated MPs, and the People's Action Party (PAP) MPs, were entirely fungible.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I do not take that consensus for granted and I express my gratitude on behalf of all my staff for your support for MFA.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And I hope it is not just because this year, MFA has regained its position as the lowest cost Ministry in the Government Budget.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, if you look at the situation of the last couple of years, it has progressively become more dangerous.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The second point, foreign policy begins at home.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Domestic unity, cohesion, consensus within and outside this House are essential for us to conduct effective foreign policy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The third point is that our foreign policy must continue to be based on a realistic assessment of our national interests and our vulnerabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It cannot be driven by sentiment, emotion or even affinities with external groups.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: When we pledge ourselves as "one united people, regardless of race, language or religion", the MFA dimension to that pledge is that when we engage with foreign countries or foreign citizens, we must also do so regardless of race, language or religion, no matter how close our hearts and our affinities are.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And this is a point that we need to bear in mind.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I was referring to the contestation between the US and China, the Russia-Ukraine war, climate change, global economic disruptions and the erosion of multilateralism.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The bifurcation, or what some people will call, decoupling, or more euphemistically, de-risking of global supply chains continues.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This type of situation is particularly worrisome for Singapore, because after all, the US and China are our major strategic investment and trading partners.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And the lack of strategic trust between them means that the risk of miscalculations that could easily spiral into a larger conflict cannot be discounted, especially over flashpoints like Taiwan and the South China Sea.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I think 2023 was the hottest year on record for 174 years.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We also stand on the precipice of a technological and economic revolution, with the advent of generative AI and even the possibility of artificial general intelligence with its impact on jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Given the appalling humanitarian tragedy, this conflict has quite understandably elicited a very strong response from both the international community as well as from Singaporeans from all walks of life, from all our communities.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It has ignited a debate over Singapore's foreign policy and how we should respond as a country.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Indeed, in this contested, fragmented and dangerous world, events in many faraway places over which we have absolutely no control will often have a profound impact on our economy and, in fact, sometimes put our domestic cohesion to the test.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, let me come back to first principles.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore's foreign policy is based on several fundamental objectives.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: First and foremost, protect our independence, sovereignty, and our territorial integrity.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Second, to secure our access to essential supplies – energy, water, food – and to keep air and sea lanes of communication open.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Third, to expand economic opportunities and to maintain our relevance to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Chong Kee Hiong have emphasised this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I want to quote the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew and the speech he gave at the S Rajaratnam lecture in 2009.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Lee said, "We have to live with the world as it is, not as we wish it to be.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We must remain nimble to seize opportunities that come with changing circumstances or to get out of harm's way".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are a small country with no hinterland, no natural resources, and in fact, no intrinsic relevance.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have to make our relevance to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have an open and trade-based economy that will always be vulnerable to external forces and trends, and we remain a multiracial, multi-religious, and multilingual society in the heart of Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: To ensure our best chances for survival, there are a few things we have to keep doing.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: First, we have to advocate for a rules-based order and full respect for international law.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is the only way that small states will have a chance to live in peace without the constant specter of invasion from bigger neighbours.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This House has just passed the Budget for the Ministry of Defence.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I stand in full support of that because, as Minister Ng said last night, we do not expect anyone to come to our rescue, to shed their blood for us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, I can even add, I do not think we can bank on any superpower exercising their right of veto in the UN Security Council on our behalf.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Sovereignty, political independence and territorial integrity is and must be sacrosanct for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we remain in fact the only Southeast Asian nation to even have sanctions in place against Russia for that egregious act.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We also spoke out against the American intervention in Grenada in 1983, and a more sensitive point closer to home, we opposed the Vietnamese invasion of Cambodia in 1978.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The reason we took these positions was not because we liked to stand out and stake out a position, but because if we had stayed quiet, we would have implicitly agreed that might makes right and that powerful states can do what they can and the weak must suffer what we must.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This goes against the very principles that undergird our existence as a sovereign, independent city-state.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But today, we are witnessing the erosion of multilateralism, we are seeing less cooperation across the world, we are seeing less unity on the global stage, less ability for the world to respond to planetary problems.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In its place, we are witnessing the rise of nationalism, of xenophobia, of protectionism, of fragmentation, and in the political arena, frankly, populism.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is inimical to Singapore domestically and to Singapore globally.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Because, in fact, if you reflect upon the past six decades of our Independence, almost six decades, we have been beneficiaries of a rules-based, integrated global economy and this has been one of the key dynamos for our success.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: International legal frameworks like the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea protect the right of all States for freedom of navigation and overflight and to maintain open sea routes and sea lines of communication.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is why Mr Vikram Nair raised the issue of the Houthi attacks in the Red Sea.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are not taking sides, but if anyone, state or non-state, for whatever excuse or pre-text, interdicts maritime safety and maritime navigation, it affects Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Members of this House may need to be reminded of our basic geography; that if you cannot navigate through the Suez Canal and the Red Sea, if that route is closed, then the shortest route between Europe and Asia around the Cape of Good Hope, is not the Straits of Malacca.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: You have to go further south and go through the Sunda Straits.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is about upholding principles, not about taking sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Second, we must make common cause with as many partners around the world as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: That means we will work with all countries on the basis of sovereign equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: To do this, we need to always bring value to the table.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our good standing today, I mean, quite frankly, my job as Foreign Minister is so much easier because I stand on the foundations laid by the Pioneer Generation who showed the world they will stand up, would not flinch, they would defend Singapore's national interest, they would add value, we would act transparently and honestly, could be relied upon to be honest brokers.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: That makes the doors open for today's generation of diplomats.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And then, we make sure that in any diplomatic conference, the Singaporean diplomats will be the most well-briefed, the most erudite, the most persuasive and the most constructive people in the room.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And the other big advantage which makes my job so much easier, is that when any Singaporean Minister or diplomat takes a stand on the international stage, it has been coordinated.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: He speaks not for himself or for MFA; he speaks for the whole-of-Government, the whole of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, this is the way we have conducted foreign policy over decades and how we have achieved a certain branding – a reputation – for being consistent, constructive and to look for win-win outcomes but on the basis of mutual respect.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So we have made a difference and we are continuing to make a difference on the international stage – whether it is frontier issues like Generative AI or climate change or digital economy, new energy or sustainability.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is these same habits and attributes that keep recurring.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And that is why we must continue to be a credible and honest partner – especially and even in the face of great power rivalry.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: That means – from time to time – we will face pressure from countries almost always bigger than us, who want us to bend to their will or at least to endorse their positions.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There is no point putting pressure on Singaporean Ministers and diplomats because if anything, we will dig in and we will hold the line even firmer.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This makes us relevant, gives us a degree of respect and ability to contribute on the global stage.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These are principles which guide – have always guided our dealings – with powers and partners, big or small.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We continue to reinforce our status as a trusted partner to both superpowers – even as we find new areas to deepen our cooperation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is important to be able to do that even whilst the two superpowers would not get along and do not have strategic trust and have not yet reached a modest-free band.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are trying to deepen cooperation and to maintain separate relationships with them that are still based on trust.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Do you understand – appreciate the nature of that diplomatic challenge?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Of course, we will continue to prioritise our relations with our neighbours – especially our two immediate neighbours, Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And, of course, with ASEAN; and with the regional players and – as I said just now – with the emerging middle powers.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I will leave Second Minister Dr Mohamad Maliki Osman and Senior Minister of State Sim Ann to give you more details on this later.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I have already mentioned the essential need for domestic cohesion and unity.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If we cannot be united at home, how do we face the outside world with all its dangers, challenges and risks?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: At Independence, we were a society riddled with racial and religious fault lines.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our forefathers overcame this by setting aside differences, not erasing it, those differences are still there.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But making sure that they did not become a source of internal tension and conflict.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our Pioneer Generation chose to put Singapore and Singaporeans first.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They worked together for the collective good to build, not a Malay nation or a Chinese nation or an Indian nation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They chose to build a nation that all of us equally could call home.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our ethnic identities, our legacies, our connections – they are still useful for maintaining friendships for establishing and expanding business connections.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But fundamentally, even as we parlay our multilingual, multicultural, multi-religious ability, we must remember to look at issues and respond as Singaporeans first.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Every time, I go to the Great Hall of the People in Beijing or the Rashtrapati Bhavan in New Delhi, I am always reminded that if my great-grandparents had not left India or China, I do not think I would be there as a guest of India or China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And then I looked around at my delegation and looked at their faces and then I always point out to my interlocutors, look at my delegation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And I speak on behalf of Singapore and Singaporeans, not as an Indian or Chinese or Malay or on the basis of my religious identity.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I am reminded of that, that every time I go to the White House or go to any palace or any Istana anywhere in the world, this is the way we have to continue dealing with all countries, both those whom we have good, friendly relations with; and those whom we may temporarily have, perhaps, a little bit of tension because of disagreements on issues.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, the point I am making, is that external issues and events will always have the potential to sow disagreement amongst us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our diversity is both a strengthen, but also that same windows of opportunity also provide windows for influence, external and for discord and divisiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So long as we remember that we must not allow centrifugal pressures to threaten our harmony and our cohesion, we can continue to take advantage of our diversity.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, it is both a defining strength and a potential source of division.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: A variety of opinions is healthy and it provides a foundation upon which we can make collective decisions as a country.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But remember that we must always find that middle ground, make the compromises arrive at the consensus, because the moment we fracture, we are irrelevant.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But there were competing narratives that were, in fact, opposed to the position that we took.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They wanted us to choose a side instead of upholding principles.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It certainly affected the price of energy, fertilisers and food.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It was part of the story of inflation around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But actually, it did not have all that much emotional resonance.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Because given our own makeup, the sense of affinity or identity is much less.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The next episode, what is happening in Gaza, the Israel-Hamas conflict.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It may actually have less – so far anyway – economic impact.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But it has got a very major emotional impact and we should recognise that.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Anyone with a heart must ache with every picture, every video, every news report you read.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Far too many innocent lives have been lost or maimed forever.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The conflict in the Middle East is a complicated one.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Or if you want to go through history, you can even go back thousands of years.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is a chronic, difficult, painful, tragic, enormously difficult to resolve problem.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Why are we so obsessed with calling out terrorism wherever we see it and we tell the world – no excuses, no pretext, no justification?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The reason we take this stand again, is not because we are taking sides or that we are trying to correct history or rewrite history.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are talking about conflict for thousands of years.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are only a country of 59 years of Independence.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We had taken that categorical stand because terrorism is a clear and present threat to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: To excuse terrorism now, for whatever reason, in fact, puts Singapore at risk.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I was thinking, if rockets landed in Bukit Panjang; if an insurgent force entered Woodlands; if 1,200 Singaporeans were killed; if 200 Singaporeans were kidnapped – that is what I was thinking of.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, when I say foreign policy begins at home, I tell you: your Foreign Minister spends more time thinking about, "What if that happens here?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: What would be the job of my diplomats and especially my Permanent Representative in New York and if we had to face the Security Council?" So, I hope you understand why we have to be so categorical at times like this, even though we know it is an emotionally fraught moment.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: After the 7 October attacks, we said we recognise Israel's right to self-defence.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Again, it is not actually because I was really thinking of Israel or taking sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We recognised Israel's right to self-defence, because we will assert Singapore's right to self-defence if we ever face a situation like that.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is not only our right of self defence, but I think Members of this House will agree it is our duty to protect our citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But even as we said there is a right of self-defence, we have consistently insisted that Israel must comply with international humanitarian law.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Israel's conduct must abide by the principles of necessity and proportionality and Israel must comply with the laws of war, including the principles of distinction and humanity enshrined in the Geneva Conventions.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For avoidance of ambiguity, I am going to repeat that line: Israel's military response has gone too far.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are also concerned that there may be a potential ground offensive into Rafa, which will only worsen the situation further.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Some people have told me that that is not enough.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We want you to sever diplomatic ties with Israel.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As a small country, this is in our national interest.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Ceremonially breaking ties with countries every time we disapprove of their actions, in my view, that is not constructive.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Whatever we say or do diplomatically will not change the situation on the ground, nor, I will add, will it influence Israel to suddenly change its policy, or will it necessarily immediately reduce the suffering on the Palestinians.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: None of the five Permanent Members of the Security Council has broken ties with Israel.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Even the Arab countries – Egypt, the UAE, Jordan – continue to have diplomatic relations with Israel.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I checked last night during a phone call.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Ambassadors may or may not be present, but their staff are present, the embassies are present, and their embassies are open and functioning.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Neither have ASEAN countries like Thailand, Philippines or Vietnam broken off relations or closed their embassies in Tel Aviv.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Ms Rachel Ong asked how Singapore's relations with Israel will be impacted by the position that we have taken on the conflict.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Clearly, they know that our position is not identical to theirs.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I would say that we have been able to maintain good and respectful relations with the State of Israel, but I would also say that we have good and equally respectful relations with the Palestinian Authority.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And all sides know that Singapore will always speak our minds, not provocatively, but because these are dearly held principles that we uphold, and that we will continue to maintain these positions guided by Singapore's long-term national interests and our unique circumstances, and whether or not you agree or disagree with us, it is not personal.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Quite frankly, I have never had to get into any shouting matches or disagreeable phone calls with any other foreign minister, regardless of circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is not because I am such an erudite and charming man, but because I am just the latest current Foreign Minister of Singapore, behaving true to form and holding fast to principles that have stood the test of time.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I want to make one more point about the Israel-Hamas conflict.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As I said just now, this is a long-standing conflict – a complicated history.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But it is worth emphasising that this is not a religious battle.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Religion is actually a veneer covering the heart of the conflict.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is an age-old conflict, a fight over land, over identity, over power.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is an issue that goes back a very long time.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And, in fact, not just by tradition, and not just because they all claim Abraham as their father, but even the latest genetic data, the Israelis and Palestinians are both – both – Semitic tribes who have been fighting over the same sliver of land for such a long time.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is not possible for outsiders like us, no matter how we feel or do not feel about them and their identity, their culture and their religion.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is not possible for Singaporeans to decide or to determine who is right or who has a stronger historical claim.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But this is only the latest chapter of a long saga of tragedy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our hearts quite rightly ache at the bloodshed.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But it is essential for Singaporeans to understand and appreciate that this is not our quarrel.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And whilst we may feel a diversity of emotions on this, the worst thing would be to let this quarrel polarise and divide us as Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is why way back in 1988 – I bet most people are not aware of that – back in 1988, we welcomed the proclamation of a Palestinian State.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are under no illusions that the path to an enduring peace will be easy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Anything else will just condemn them to repeating the cycles of violence and tragedy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, we have consistently expressed our support for a two-state solution at the UN.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have consistently opposed moves that undermine a two-state solution in Israel and Palestine.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
